title: COSHH & hazardous substances
blurb: Hazard pictograms, safety data sheets, COSHH assessments and the hierarchy of control for the chemicals you use every day.
question: A new surface disinfectant arrives with a red-bordered diamond on the label showing liquid eating into a hand. A colleague wants to pour some into an old unlabelled spray bottle to make it easier to use. What must happen before anyone uses the product, and what is wrong with decanting it?

teach.body: The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH) require employers to prevent, or adequately control, exposure to substances that can harm health. In a dental practice that includes disinfectants, acid etchant, mercury and amalgam, alcohol-based wipes, acrylic monomer, radiograph processing chemicals, bleaching agents, natural rubber latex, and biological agents such as blood-borne viruses. Your employer assesses the risks; you follow the controls and report problems.

teach.caption: Under the CLP (GB) rules, hazard pictograms are a black symbol on a white diamond with a red border. They replaced the old orange square symbols.

teach.body: Every hazardous product comes with a safety data sheet (SDS) from the supplier. It is the key source of hazard information: what the hazards are, safe handling and storage, the PPE needed, first aid, what to do with a spill, and how to dispose of it. Safety data sheets must be kept where staff can get to them quickly, and the COSHH assessment is built from them. The label on the container gives the short version.

levels.label: Administrative controls

teach.caption: Work down from the top. PPE only protects the wearer and only when worn correctly, so it is the last line of defence.

teach.h: Everyday safe use: do or don't?

rows.label: Keep in the original labelled container
Decant into an unlabelled spray bottle
Mix two products to make them stronger
Follow the dilution on the label
Leave caps loose for quick access

teach.note: Mixing products can cause dangerous reactions and toxic gases. An unlabelled bottle found in use should be removed from use and dealt with under the COSHH procedure.

teach.body: Eye splash: rinse immediately with plenty of clean water or an eyewash, follow the SDS first aid advice and the emergency procedure, then get medical help and report it. Dizziness or headache from vapours: stop the exposure, get to fresh air and report it. Skin irritation: report it so it can be assessed, as it may be occupational dermatitis. Spills: follow the spill procedure for that product (such as developer solution) using the right PPE and spill kit.

Natural rubber latex is a sensitiser: repeated exposure can cause skin reactions and, in some people, asthma or anaphylaxis. If a team member develops a latex allergy, the right response is to provide latex-free alternatives (such as nitrile gloves) and review the risk assessment, not to make them cope with liners or creams. Ask patients about latex allergy in the medical history too, and plan a latex-free appointment for them.

teach.text: PPE is the LAST line of defence, not the first. If an exam question asks which control to consider before relying on PPE, the answer is elimination or substitution.

items: COSHH 2002: assess and control exposure to hazardous substances.
The SDS is the key hazard document; keep it accessible.
New product: read SDS, assess, decide controls, train, then use. Review if reformulated.
Hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, PPE last.
Original labelled containers, lids closed, never mix, follow dilutions, ventilate.
Latex allergy: latex-free alternatives and review the risk assessment.

summary: You can now recognise the CLP hazard pictograms, explain what a safety data sheet tells you, follow the sequence for introducing a new product, apply the hierarchy of control, and respond safely to splashes, vapours, spills and latex allergy.

A.q: A new surface disinfectant has been delivered. Which document gives the key information about its hazards?
options: The delivery note
The safety data sheet
The stock order form
The practice risk register
A.why: The supplier's safety data sheet sets out the hazards, safe handling, PPE, first aid, spillage and disposal.

whyNot.0: A delivery note confirms what arrived, not how hazardous it is.
whyNot.2: Stock forms track quantities and ordering.
whyNot.3: A risk register summarises practice risks but is not the product's hazard source.

A.q: A COSHH assessment is being completed for a new disinfectant. Which control should be considered BEFORE relying on PPE?
options: Revising written procedures
Health surveillance for staff
Eliminating or substituting it
Putting up warning signs
A.why: The hierarchy of control starts with elimination and substitution, which remove or reduce the hazard at source.

whyNot.0: Procedures are administrative controls, lower in the hierarchy.
whyNot.1: Health surveillance checks for harm; it doesn't prevent exposure.
whyNot.3: Signs are administrative controls and rely on people reading them.

A.q: A bottle of disinfectant is found decanted into an unlabelled spray bottle. What is the best action?
options: Use it up, then wash out the bottle
Relabel it using your best guess
Store it with the other cleaning products for now
Remove it from use; follow COSHH procedure
A.why: An unlabelled chemical's hazards and strength are unknown. Remove it from use and follow the local COSHH procedure.

whyNot.0: Using an unidentified chemical could cause harm or a dangerous reaction.
whyNot.1: Guessing the contents could put a false and dangerous label on it.
whyNot.2: Storing it keeps an unidentified hazard in circulation.

B.q: Which hazard pictogram would you expect on a bottle of phosphoric acid etchant?
options: Corrosive
Gas under pressure
Explosive
Environmental hazard
B.why: Acid etchant can burn skin and damage eyes, so it carries the corrosive pictogram.

whyNot.1: Gas under pressure applies to cylinders such as oxygen.
whyNot.3: The environmental pictogram is typical of mercury and amalgam.

B.q: The practice is switching to a different disinfectant. Which sequence is correct?
options: Train staff, use it, then record the assessment
Read the SDS, assess, train staff, then use it
Order it, use it, then complete the assessment
Trial it once, then decide whether to assess
B.why: Hazard information comes first, then the risk assessment and controls, then training, and only then use.

whyNot.0: Training must be based on the assessment, which must come before use.
whyNot.2: The assessment must be done before anyone is exposed.
whyNot.3: Trialling an unassessed product exposes staff to unknown risks.

B.q: A team member feels dizzy after using a strong cleaning product in a small room. What should they do?
options: Finish quickly, then take a break
Open a window and keep going
Stop, get to fresh air and report it
Switch to a weaker product and carry on
B.why: Dizziness suggests over-exposure to vapour. Stop the exposure, get fresh air, and report it so controls can be reviewed.

whyNot.1: Ventilation helps, but they must stop and leave the exposure first.
whyNot.3: The incident must still be reported and the assessment reviewed.

C.q: A nurse develops a latex allergy. What is the most appropriate response from the practice?
options: Ask them to wear cotton liners under their latex gloves
Move them to reception duties permanently
Suggest antihistamines before each session
Provide latex-free gloves and review the assessment
C.why: Substituting latex-free products removes the hazard at source, and the risk assessment must be updated.

whyNot.0: Liners don't stop exposure to latex proteins.
whyNot.1: Removing them from clinical work is unnecessary when substitution works.
whyNot.2: Medication masks symptoms; it does not control exposure.

C.q: A supplier tells the practice that a disinfectant has been reformulated. What must be reviewed?
options: The COSHH assessment for that product
The waste transfer notes
The fire risk assessment
The staff rota for the decontamination room
C.why: A new formulation can change the hazards, so the COSHH assessment and its controls must be reviewed.

whyNot.1: Waste transfer notes record waste collection, not product hazards.
whyNot.2: The fire risk assessment would only change if fire risk changed; the COSHH assessment is the priority.
whyNot.3: Rotas don't address the product's new hazards.

C.q: Which statement about mixing two cleaning products together is correct?
options: It is fine if both are disinfectants
It may cause a dangerous chemical reaction
It makes the products more effective
It is acceptable if well diluted with water afterwards
C.why: Mixing chemicals can produce heat or toxic gases. Never mix products unless the manufacturer says to.

whyNot.0: Two disinfectants can still react dangerously together.
whyNot.2: Mixing doesn't improve effectiveness and may destroy it.
whyNot.3: Dilution afterwards doesn't undo a reaction that has already happened.

reteach.title: Think of a chemical like a guard dog
reteach.question: A guard dog can be dangerous, but it is safe if it is known, labelled, fenced in and handled by trained people. How does that map to COSHH?

blocks.h: Know it, fence it, train for it
blocks.body: The safety data sheet is the dog's file: what it does and how to handle it. The label and pictogram are the 'Beware of the dog' sign. The best control is not having a dangerous dog at all (elimination) or getting a calmer breed (substitution). Next, build a strong fence (engineering controls like ventilation). Then set rules and train people (administrative controls). Thick gloves (PPE) are the last resort if all else fails.

blocks.text: An unlabelled bottle is like a dog with no file: you don't know how dangerous it is. Never use it. Remove it from use.

explain.body: Hazard pictograms are red-bordered diamonds that show the type of hazard at a glance. The safety data sheet gives the full detail: hazards, handling, storage, PPE, first aid, spills and disposal.

test.q: Alcohol-based surface wipes are most likely to carry which pictogram?
options: Corrosive
Flammable
Explosive
Oxidising
test.why: Alcohol is highly flammable, so alcohol-based wipes carry the flame pictogram.

whyNot.0: Corrosive is for substances that burn skin or metal, such as acids.
whyNot.3: Oxidisers feed a fire with oxygen; alcohol is a fuel.

explain.body: The assessment identifies the substance's hazards, who could be exposed and how, and the controls needed. It is done before use and reviewed when a product is changed or reformulated, after an incident, or if someone's health is affected. Staff must be trained on the substances they use.

test.q: Why should staff be trained on the hazardous substances they use?
options: To meet the insurer's conditions
To use less product each month
To understand the risks and safe methods
To remove the need for safety data sheets
test.why: Training means staff know the hazards and how to work safely with each substance.

whyNot.0: Insurance is not the purpose of COSHH training.
whyNot.1: Saving product is not the aim.
whyNot.3: Safety data sheets are still required and must be accessible.

explain.body: Eliminate, substitute, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE. Higher controls remove or reduce the hazard for everyone; lower controls depend on people doing the right thing every time.

test.q: Installing extraction ventilation in the decontamination room is an example of which control?
options: Substitution
Administrative control
Personal protective equipment
Engineering control
test.why: Ventilation and extraction are engineering controls: they reduce exposure at source through the building or equipment.

whyNot.0: Substitution means swapping to a safer substance.
whyNot.1: Administrative controls are procedures, training and signs.
whyNot.2: PPE is worn by the person, such as gloves or masks.

explain.h: Safe storage and exposure first aid
explain.body: Keep products in their original labelled containers with lids closed, stored as the SDS says. Never mix products. Eye splash: rinse immediately and follow the emergency procedure. Vapours: stop exposure, fresh air, report. Skin irritation: report for assessment.

test.q: Disinfectant splashes into a nurse's eye while she is decanting it. What should happen first?
options: Wipe the eye with sterile gauze
Rinse the eye immediately with water
Look up the product's SDS first
Report it before doing anything
test.why: Immediate, thorough rinsing limits damage. The SDS, reporting and medical help follow.

whyNot.0: Wiping can spread the chemical and damage the eye.
whyNot.2: Delay allows more damage; rinse first, then check the SDS.
